lede: From the appointment of the chief engineer to the Overseas Highway. Until the modules are carried, each station names the source it rests on; figures are given as that source gives them.

stations.text: Joseph Carroll Meredith takes up his duty as chief constructing engineer of the extension. Work on the keys begins in April 1905 under his charge.
stations.src: Florida East Coast Railway, Key West Extension … opened January 22, 1912 (1912)

stations.text: Scientific American reports that the railway's engineers have completed plans and surveys for a line to Key West over the keys: a harbour 33 feet deep, a car ferry to Havana, and the port nearest the Panama Canal.

Men at the camp on the east end of Key West strike and march to the city hall to demand food. The town feeds them for two days; the business men force them back to work, and a few serve terms as vagrants on the streets.

stations.titel: The quarterboats are carried out to sea
stations.text: A hurricane tears the workers' quarterboats from their moorings. The Weather Bureau's offices report the dead as 'probably more than 100', 'about 135' and '124'; forty-nine men are picked up by the Austrian steamer Jenny.

About 2,800 labourers are at work, four-fifths of them white. They are recruited in New York, Philadelphia and Boston; the fare south is deducted from their wages, and about one in four deserts on the way.
stations.src: F. E. Spooner, Railroad Gazette 42 (26 April 1907)

stations.text: Labour agents and engineers of the line are tried in the federal court at New York on charges of peonage. The trial ends in acquittal.
stations.src: Railway Age Gazette 52 (10 May 1912), p. 1041; Associated Press, 13 November 1908

stations.titel: The Immigration Commission in the camps
stations.text: A member of the federal Immigration Commission visits every camp. The Commission finds 'some coercion' in the early days and foremen dismissed for it, but no legal proof of peonage.
stations.src: Reports of the Immigration Commission, Abstracts, vol. 2 (1911), pp. 445–446

stations.text: The chief constructing engineer dies on duty. William J. Krome completes the work.
A hurricane strikes the steel bridge under construction at Knight's Key; spans are blown from their piers. The company afterwards decides to build more miles of concrete arches in place of fill.
stations.src: Engineering Record 61 (2 April 1910); Railway Age Gazette 52 (1912)

stations.titel: The first train at Key West
stations.text: Flagler's train arrives at Key West over the sea. The company's booklet puts the line at 128.4 miles from Homestead, with 17.2 miles of bridges, and calls it 'of practically storm-proof construction'.
The Florida East Coast Railway defaults on the interest of its second mortgage and passes into the hands of receivers.

The hurricane crosses the Upper Keys. A train of eleven cars sent from Miami to bring out the veterans is washed from the track; the Red Cross puts the dead at 409, of whom 244 known dead and 165 missing.
stations.src: W. F. McDonald, Monthly Weather Review 63 (September 1935), pp. 269–271

stations.text: The Interstate Commerce Commission permits the railway to abandon the line south of Florida City. Rebuilding is judged not practicable.
The State has bought the right of way and the bridges for $640,000 out of a federal loan of $3,500,000. Concrete road bridges are built 'on the piers of the old railroad bridges'.
stations.src: C. R. Vinten, The Regional Review (National Park Service) 1 (July 1938)
